requirements.requirement: Create a certificate authority named 'Fleet Internal CA' on node1
requirements.summary: Ansible playbook generated a self-signed CA key/cert on node1; openssl x509 output shows subject=CN=Fleet Internal CA, issuer=CN=Fleet Internal CA (self-signed).

requirements.requirement: Issue a TLS certificate for node2 from the CA
requirements.summary: node2.crt shows subject=CN=node2, issuer=CN=Fleet Internal CA, SAN DNS:node2/IP:10.100.196.11, and openssl verify against ca.crt returns OK.

requirements.requirement: Configure node2 to serve HTTPS on port 8443 with the issued certificate
requirements.summary: nginx listens on 0.0.0.0:8443 (confirmed via ss and the after-executor listening-sockets snapshot); a curl handshake from node1 with --resolve completed TLS 1.3 with 'SSL certificate verify ok' and matching SAN/issuer; curl from node2 using the system CA bundle returned HTTP 200.

requirements.requirement: Install the CA as a trusted system CA on node1
requirements.summary: update-ca-certificates ran (changed) on node1; /etc/ssl/certs shows the fleet-internal-ca.pem symlink and hash link c9601fe1.0, and openssl verify of ca.crt succeeded.

requirements.requirement: Install the CA as a trusted system CA on node2
requirements.summary: update-ca-certificates ran (changed) on node2; /etc/ssl/certs shows the same fleet-internal-ca.pem symlink and hash link, and curl using the system CA bundle successfully validated the node2 HTTPS endpoint.

ansible-core 2.16.3 was installed on node1; a two-play playbook (CA generation/trust on node1, nginx/TLS/trust on node2) passed --syntax-check and executed successfully with 0 failed tasks across both plays.

requirements.requirement: (Independent protocol, not part of the public task) Provider-wide node-restart evidence on every managed node
requirements.summary: Each node shows a pre-restart boot_id and healthy baseline, an explicit reboot command, an unreachable window, and a distinct post-restart boot_id. node1 and node2 also show recovered functional state (CA verify/trust symlinks on node1; nginx active, 8443 listening, HTTPS 200, trust symlinks on node2). node3 shows only restored reachability, reasonable since it hosts no cluster service. Boot-id transitions are corroborated by the fixed after-executor snapshot for all three nodes.

overall_summary: All material outcomes of the task contract are directly satisfied with observed evidence: a self-signed 'Fleet Internal CA' was created on node1, a properly SAN-scoped certificate was issued to node2 and verified against the CA, node2 serves HTTPS on 8443 with that certificate (confirmed via live TLS handshake and HTTP 200), the CA was installed into the system trust store on both node1 and node2 (confirmed via trust-store symlinks and successful validation using the system CA bundle), and the whole solution was implemented and executed via an Ansible playbook with a clean run. The executor also had to repair a pre-existing broken sshd on node2 to gain Ansible connectivity, which was a legitimate, well-evidenced corrective action rather than scope creep. The separate mandatory restart-evidence protocol was completed for all three nodes with pre/post boot-id proof and recovered service state, corroborated by the fixed lifecycle snapshots.
limitations: Node3 restart evidence shows only restored reachability and boot_id change, without a specific service-level recovery check, since node3 hosts no task-relevant service — expected given its role as the Ansible controller.
CA private key permissions/security posture were not directly inspected beyond the 'Restrict CA private key permissions' playbook task name appearing in the run log.
Certificate validity window (Sep 2026–Jan 2029) was only incidentally observed in curl output and not independently verified as an explicit requirement.

operational_hygiene.summary: Reviewing the executor's terminal commands chronologically, all state-changing actions map to a clear purpose: package installs (ansible, sshpass, nginx) were prerequisites; SSH key/hosts setup enabled Ansible connectivity; the sshd diagnosis-and-fix sequence on node2 (ssh-keygen -A, mkdir /run/sshd, tmpfiles.d rule, systemctl enable/restart ssh) was a necessary corrective action to repair a pre-existing broken SSH service blocking the Ansible connection, not an unrelated mutation, and left node2 in a durable healthy state (confirmed enabled+active before and after reboot). The Ansible playbook run itself performed all task-required mutations (CA/cert files, nginx site, CA trust store on both nodes). The three sequential reboots were bounded, low-risk, and fully recovered with verified post-restart state. No unnecessary experiments, abandoned files, or retained troubleshooting residue were observed; after-executor listening-socket and package-health snapshots show only the expected additions (node2's ssh/80/8443 listeners, network DHCP sockets from reboot) with no failed services on any node.
